results.title: Nebius to Increase AI Cloud Service Prices Again This October | Tech Pulse | TheNextGenTechInsider
highlights:
# Nebius to Increase AI Cloud Service Prices Again This October

Amsterdam-based Nebius will implement its second price hike in three months starting October 1, 2026. The adjustments target GPU instances, CPU configurations, and memory services due to high demand.

Hiren Dave

Founder

Sep 27, 2026• 4 min read

### KEY TAKEAWAYS

Rates for selected graphics processing units will increase between 17% and 21% as reported by Reuters.

On-demand rates for certain CPU instances, including those powered by AMD and Intel architectures, will rise by 25% according to Reuters.

Memory Offerings

Prices for memory-intensive services are expected to increase by approximately 41% as noted in Reuters.

Increasing to $9.50 per GPU-hour per Nebius pricing data.

## Nebius Announces Second Price Increase for AI Cloud Services in Three Months

Amsterdam-based cloud provider Nebius has announced a scheduled price increase for its pay-as-you-go services, effective October 1, 2026, according to official pricing documentation. This marks the company's second rate hike within a three-month period, following a previous adjustment in May 2026. The move comes amid surging global demand for computing capacity required to train and deploy large-scale AI models.

The price adjustments reflect broader market pressures in the AI infrastructure sector, where demand for high-performance compute continues to outpace the deployment of new GPU supply. This trend is mirrored by industry competitors, such as CoreWeave, which reported similar upward pricing trends for high-demand hardware.

## Technical Specifications and Pricing Adjustments

The upcoming price changes affect a wide range of compute and memory resources. The most significant adjustments are applied to NVIDIA GPU instances and CPU-only configurations:

- NVIDIA GPU Instances: Rates for selected graphics processing units will increase between 17% and 21% as reported by Reuters.
- CPU-only Instances: On-demand rates for certain CPU instances, including those powered by AMD and Intel architectures, will rise by 25% according to Reuters.
- Memory Offerings: Prices for memory-intensive services are expected to increase by approximately 41% as noted in Reuters.

 Specific upcoming rates for high-end hardware include: 

- NVIDIA HGX B300: Increasing to $9.50 per GPU-hour per Nebius pricing data.
- NVIDIA HGX B200: Increasing to $8.50 per GPU-hour per Nebius pricing data.
- NVIDIA HGX H200: Increasing to $5.40 per GPU-hour per Nebius pricing data.
- NVIDIA HGX H100: Increasing to $4.50 per GPU-hour per Nebius pricing data.

## Cost Mitigation Strategies

To offset these increases, Nebius continues to offer commitment-based pricing models. Customers who reserve large-scale clusters for multiple months can access commitment discounts of up to 35% compared to standard on-demand rates as detailed in the Nebius pricing guide. Additionally, the provider maintains preemptible (spot) pricing options for fault-tolerant workloads, which allows for more cost-effective utilization of available capacity.

The price hike follows a period of rapid expansion for Nebius's AI cloud business, during which the company secured four major customer contracts averaging over $1 billion each according to Reuters. This growth highlights the increasing reliance of enterprises on specialized "neocloud" providers for mission-critical AI training and inference workloads.

results.title: The Blackwell shortage playbook: finding B200/B300 capacity without paying the hyperscaler premium — CheapestGPU
highlights:
The binding constraint is packaging, not wafers. Troy Technical's August 9, 2026 report on the CoWoS bottleneck states TSMC CEO C.C. Wei confirmed in June 2026 that CoWoS-L advanced-packaging capacity remained "extremely tight and sold out through 2026," even as TSMC targets 125,000 to 130,000 wafers/month by year-end. The same report puts Nvidia's 2026 CoWoS bookings at roughly 800,000 to 850,000 wafers, about 60% of TSMC's total output on Morgan Stanley's estimate, locking in packaging for Blackwell Ultra (B300) and next-generation Rubin silicon at the same time. CoWoS demand is running 40 to 50 percent above supply, and enterprise buyers are seeing Blackwell delivery slip into Q1 2027 because packaging allocation, not wafer supply, is the ceiling.

That packaging squeeze shows up directly in list prices. Shattered's 2026 report on Nebius' pricing states the neocloud raised GPU rental rates by up to 21% effective October 1, 2026 - B300 from $7.85 to $9.50/GPU-hr (about 21%), B200 from $7.15 to $8.50/GPU-hr (about 19%). It is Nebius' second hike in 2026: an earlier May pass raised on-demand rates roughly 29% and spot rates roughly 51%, so the current B300 rate sits about 56% above its pre-May level of roughly $6.10/GPU-hr. Read that as market context on where hyperscaler-adjacent neocloud pricing is heading, not as a CheapestGPU board rate.

## The neocloud vs hyperscaler spread

Thunder Compute's September 2026 B200 pricing pass, tracking 11 providers, put the on-demand floor at $5.99/GPU-hr (Hyperbolic) against a $16.11/GPU-hr ceiling (Google Cloud) - a single B200 running 24/7 for a month costs about $4,313 at the floor versus $11,599 at the ceiling, a spread of roughly 2.7x for the same silicon. That comparison is cited market data, useful for orienting yourself, but it is not a CheapestGPU listing.

The order book carries exactly two live B200 rows today, and both are SXM, 36-month reserved, 20% prepayment - there is no PCIe or on-demand B200 row on the board right now:

- `io-b200-512-2026` (`data/listingsIo.ts`): 512x B200 SXM, $3.84/GPU-hr, NVLink 5 / NVSwitch intra-node, IB-ready NDR400 (CX-7 VPI) inter-node, location "Reserved - RFS TBD", proposal-backed (`IO-B200-512-2026`), $10,333,716.48 prepayment at signing. At the board's 730-hours/month baseline: $3.84 x 730 = $2,803/GPU/month; the full 512-GPU row is $2,803 x 512 = ~$1,435,238/month.
- `cap-b200-256-hot-2026` (`data/listingsBaremetal.ts`): 256x B200 SXM, $3.85/GPU-hr, Full NDR InfiniBand + leaf/spine + OOB management, Tier III datacenter (location TBD), capacity-board row with no attachment, $4,843,929.60 prepayment at signing. At 730 hours/month: $3.85 x 730 = $2,810.50/GPU/month; the full 256-GPU row is $719,488/month.

Both rows carry the same commitment shape (SXM, 36 months, 20% down), so the "spread" claim above cannot be compared sticker-to-sticker against them - it is an hourly on-demand rate against a signed multi-year reserved price. Compare like commitment types, not like GPU models.

...

Using the two real B200 rows above against Thunder Compute's cited on-demand band: $2,803/$4,313 (neocloud floor) is about 65%, and $2,803/$11,599 (hyperscaler ceiling) is about 24%. The `cap-b200-256-hot-2026` row lands at nearly the same ratios ($2,810.50/$4,313 and $2,810.50/$11,599). In plain terms: if you would run this capacity more than about two-thirds of the term hours, either board reserved rate beats even the cheapest tracked neocloud on-demand price; against the hyperscaler ceiling, breakeven drops under a quarter utilization. The catch is the term floor - both rows require signing 36 months with 20% down to get there. Neither can be signed for 30 or 90 days; a shorter job has to go through on-demand or a custom term negotiated over Message.

results.title: Best GPU Cloud Providers for AI Startups in 2026: Real H100 and B200 Prices - Startupik
highlights:
The best GPU cloud for most AI startups in 2026 is a self-serve neocloud, not a hyperscaler. RunPod ($3.49 per H100 hour) and Lambda ($3.99) are the cheapest verified on-demand options for a single H100. Modal wins for bursty, serverless inference. Together AI wins when you can commit for 3 to 6 months. CoreWeave, AWS and Google only make sense once you need full 8-GPU nodes or already hold their credits.

One date matters right now. Nebius raises its on-demand prices on 1 October 2026, and most “cheapest GPU” lists have not caught up.

Last reviewed: September 2026

## Quick Verdict: Which GPU Cloud Should a Startup Pick?

- Cheapest single H100: RunPod Secure Cloud H100 SXM at $3.49 per hour, billed by the second, per RunPod’s pricing page.
- Price change to plan for: Nebius H100 goes from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour on 1 October 2026, and B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, per Nebius’s price page.
- Cheapest verified B200: Modal at $6.25 per hour of GPU time, followed by Lambda at $6.69.
- Best commitment discount with a public rate card: Together AI H100 falls from $3.99 on demand to $3.19 on a 91–180 day reservation.
- Minimum-unit trap: CoreWeave sells H100 only as an 8-GPU node at $49.24 per hour, which is $35,945 for a month of 24/7 use.
- Biggest free credits: Google for Startups offers up to $350,000 for AI startups, but only $250,000 of it lands in year one.

...

Two things changed in September. First, GPU clouds became a public-market story. Nscale filed for a NYSE listing under the ticker NSCL on 18 September 2026, according to its own press release. Its filing shows H1 2026 revenue of $140.6M and a net loss of $1.02B, as reported by TradingView and Dealroom. It also shows statements of work with Microsoft (up to about $43.8B) and Anthropic (up to about $44.6B).

That tells you where capacity goes. The largest buyers sign multi-year contracts. Nscale publishes no public GPU prices at all; every H100 and GB300 page ends in “Get a quote” or “Contact sales”.

Second, prices are moving up at the self-serve end. Nebius, which offers no-commitment self-service up to 32 GPUs, lifts its on-demand rate card by 17% to 21% on 1 October. Any article or spreadsheet quoting $3.85 per H100 hour will be wrong within days.

For a seed-stage team, the practical question is no longer “who has H100s?” It is “who sells me one GPU, by the second, without a sales call, at a price that will still hold next quarter?”

## How Did We Compare These GPU Clouds?

We read every provider’s official pricing page in September 2026. Where a price is listed per node, we divided it by the GPU count and show both. Where a provider does not publish a price, we say so instead of estimating.

H100 here means the NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM part unless noted. B200 is NVIDIA’s Blackwell data-centre GPU. A neocloud is a GPU-first cloud provider, such as Lambda or CoreWeave, as opposed to a general hyperscaler like AWS.

### 3. Nebius: Strong Today, Repriced on 1 October

Why it works: Nebius offers self-serve access up to 32 GPUs with “no waitlists or minimum commitments”, after a $25 top-up. It publishes preemptible prices from $0.79 for H100 and H200 and from $0.99 for B200 and B300, the lowest spot entry points in this list.

When it breaks: The new rate card takes effect on 1 October 2026:

After the change, Nebius H100 is more expensive than Lambda, Together and RunPod on demand. Nebius is also the only provider here with a published egress fee: $0.015 per GiB for Standard object storage. Its startup credits are “currently available exclusively through” partner VC funds, for companies with $5M+ raised.

Use it if your workloads tolerate preemption, or you will negotiate a multi-month reservation (Nebius says up to 35% below on-demand). Skip it as your default on-demand provider after 1 October.

Why it works: Together publishes the full commitment ladder, which almost nobody else does.

### 6. CoreWeave: Built for Clusters, Priced per Node

Why it works: CoreWeave is the reference neocloud for serious multi-node training. It lists HGX H100 at $49.24 per hour, HGX B200 at $68.80 and GB200 NVL72 at $42.00 per 4-GPU instance. Egress is free, and it promises “up to 60% discounts” for committed usage.

When it breaks: The price is per node, not per GPU. The H100 node works out to $6.16 per GPU, about 54% above Lambda. More importantly, you cannot rent one GPU. A single always-on H100 workload that costs $2,548 a month on RunPod means renting a $35,945 node on CoreWeave.

Also note the GB200 row: it is 4 GPUs per instance, not 8. Comparisons that divide by eight report $5.25 per GPU instead of the correct $10.50.

Use it if you train across many nodes and can negotiate a commitment. Skip it before you have a workload that fills eight GPUs.

results.title: Vera Rubin is 10× more efficient. You still can’t rent it cheap.
highlights:
The first Vera Rubin cloud instances are live — CoreWeave, Google Cloud’s A5X, Azure, OCI and Nebius are ramping them now, with production spinning up across NVIDIA’s partners. The number everyone is quoting is “10× lower cost per token than Blackwell.” It’s a real result and a big deal for the industry — but if you’re deciding whether to rent or buy for your own inference, it does not mean what it sounds like, and it will not show up on your bill this quarter.

The newest GPU is never the cheapest to rent. The per-hour ladder rises with each generation; Rubin lands premium and price-unknown. The efficiency win reaches you indirectly.

...

NVIDIA’s claim is precisely “~10× more tokens per megawatt” and “one-tenth the cost per million tokens” versus a GB200 NVL72 rack; CoreWeave independently reports ~10× the tokens/second per megawatt. Notice the unit: this is an energy-efficiency figure at the rack level, not a rental price. It becomes a 10× cost reduction only when power is your dominant cost and the rack is fully utilized — the vendor’s best case. No cloud has published a Rubin $/hour or $/token rate, and there’s a reason: first-wave supply is scarce and hyperscaler-reserved, with TSMC’s CoWoS packaging sold out until roughly Q4 2026. A launch-generation part is always priced at a premium while it’s rationed.

## The newest GPU is never the cheapest to rent

Look at the ladder. Today’s neocloud medians run about $2.00/hr for an A100, $4.17 for an H100, $4.50 for an H200, $7.88 for a B200, and ~$12 for a still-scarce B300. Each newer generation launched more expensive per hour, not less — because you’re paying for scarcity and peak demand, and the efficiency gains are amortized by the operator over time. Rubin will slot in at the top of that ladder, not the bottom. “Newest = cheapest per token” is true in a datacenter’s power budget; it is false on a rental invoice for months after launch.

results.title: AI chips are in demand. The debt still matters.
highlights:
Companies can rent AI chips by the hour. A rising rental price suggests that access is getting more valuable, at least within the market being measured.

Here is the September 23 snapshot attributed to Ornn, in dollars per chip-hour:

- B200: $7.95, roughly 79% above June 24 and a high within the available three-month window.
- H200: $5.01, up about 50%.
- H100: $3.05, up about 30%.
- A100: $1.03, up about 1%.

The strength was concentrated in newer hardware. The older A100 had barely moved.

We checked the public data again. It now returns $5.02 for H200 on September 23; the other three prices match. June 24 has rolled out of the public history, so those original percentage changes remain historical readings we could not reproduce. [1]

Our chart uses every available daily observation from June 27 through September 25. Over that slightly different period, B200 rose 82% to $8.04, H200 42% to $5.08, H100 13% to $2.85, and A100 3% to $1.02.

Prices also fell hard along the way. B200 dropped 22% between July 14 and August 10. H200 lost 25% between July 31 and August 26. On September 23, H200 remained about 11% below its July high.

There is no single price for the whole rental market. Silicon Data’s reported September 24 readings were $5.45–$5.77 for B200, $3.31 for H200, $2.61 for H100, and $1.57 for A100. Different contracts, configurations, and providers produce different benchmarks. Those earlier displays are historical observations; we could not recreate them all. [2]

Ornn measures on-demand rentals. It excludes long-term reservations, has a short history, and also sells compute reservations. Its index is useful evidence from a limited market. A second vendor’s price level does not independently confirm its trend.

...

A higher price means more when customers keep taking the available capacity.

Ornn’s reported seven-day averages through September 23 put B200 at roughly 97% rented, up from about 60% in early August. H200 went from roughly 69% in late August to 90%. H100 was near 85%. B200 and H200 had both been around 40% in mid-June. [3]

We could verify the price series, but not the underlying utilization readings. These are vendor-reported historical figures. They cover tracked rental capacity, not all chips worldwide or how hard each processor is working.

...

Its September 17 update again reported higher prices for new contracts. Nebius has also posted higher on-demand hourly rates effective October 1: B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, H200 from $4.50 to $5.40, H100 from $3.85 to $4.50, and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. These are company-specific observations, but they make a blanket claim of falling rental prices hard to defend. [20]

...

Rental data [1–3]. ... Our chart uses June 27–September 25. Historical June 24 comparisons and utilization remain unreproduced. The live Silicon pages had moved to B200 $5.87 and H100 $2.72 dated September 26, H200 $3.30 dated September 24, and A100 $1.57 without a separately confirmed date.
